title: How i built an AI-Powered travel app that makes research and planning fast and fun
intro: Vayo introduces a better way to find places you love, plan your trip with ease and manage all your maps and pins in one place. I owned the whole path alone and did all research, design and building the app with AI in just one month.

blocks.title: Learning how far AI can go, by building something I needed
paras: I started this project to find out how to best integrate AI into the design process and use it as much as possible, in every step and with the best possible output. I used that learning process to build a product that solves frustrations I have had for years.
I used AI in more than [[40 different steps]] of this project, from mapping assumptions and applying multi-agent problem lenses to creating the full 133-page clickable prototype in just one day.
I set clear rules and boundaries to always get high-quality output. The whole process is automatically documented, and **every decision can be traced back to the data behind it**.

blocks.text: Main tools
Frustrations with Google MyMaps

After using Google's MyMaps to plan all my trip for years, i was very frustrated with its limitations. So i wanted to build my own app that lifts the limitations and adds AI-Powered research capabilities.

items.name: p3
items.title: Pictures break over time
items.text: Photos on a pin only link to outside sources. When a link changes, the picture is gone, and the pin no longer tells me what it was. In a test on a two-year-old map, more than a third of the images had disappeared.

items.name: p2
items.title: Drive times are buried in turn-by-turn directions
items.text: The time for a leg sits between cryptic driving instructions. With routes for more than one day squeezed into one layer, the relevant times had to be extracted and added up manually.

items.name: p1
items.title: Limits for layers and pins per route
items.text: In MyMaps there are only 10 layers available to manage all your pins, routes and collections, which quickly run out. It's not possible to plan trips longer than a week without applying some workarounds.

items.name: p4
items.title: No built-in research capabilities. So every find comes from elsewhere
items.text: MyMaps can't search for places. Every find had to come in from other apps and be added by hand, one pin at a time.

blocks.text: Started building the live app in parallel with the user interviews

Along with the traditional user interviews I started building the app itself, beginning with a brain-dumped concept of what an MVP needs. Its first versions tested the riskiest assumptions: how precisely free services place pins, how good the research results are and how good the image sources are. I wrote down what I learned. Later I combined the interview insights, those learnings and the initial concept into a new concept. The clickable prototype grew out of it, and the app now catches up with what the prototype added.

blocks.name: testapp
blocks.title: Testing the feasibility of the core features live
blocks.text: In the first version of the app I tested the riskiest assumptions: how precisely free services place pins, how good the quality of the built-in research could be and where to source the best images.
From interviews to insights

I ran six interviews about how people plan trips and broke the transcripts down into 134 individual observations, each tied to the participant’s own words. I sorted these on an affinity map into motivation clusters and pain-point clusters. Every cluster had to hold up across at least two different people, otherwise it counted as a single voice, not a pattern. From the surviving clusters I drew about twenty insights and cut each one back to the part the quotes actually support. They merged into 18 insights, which became the basis for the need statement and the problem statement.

blocks.label: How AI was involved
blocks.text: I used AI to clean the raw interview transcripts, pull candidate observations out of them, and draft the first clustering and the first set of insights. **AI did the heavy lifting on volume, and I stayed in charge of what counted as evidence.**
One funnel, spread across many tools

Planning is a funnel from many finds to a shortlist to day-sized routes, and each step lives in a different tool. Every hand-off between those tools costs time, and some of what I found gets lost on the way, so I end up sorting the same pins twice.
Refining the concept with what I learned

I brought three things together: what the interviews showed about how people plan, what the test app proved about pins, research and photos, and the funnel from the key insight. Then I used AI to push the concept further. It came up with five different concepts, I checked them against each other and rated each one on desirability, viability and feasibility, and the result is the one I built: find, shortlist, plan the days.

blocks.label: How AI helped
blocks.text: AI generated the five concepts, rated them, and hunted for dead ends and edge cases in the flow. I chose the direction and made the final call on every decision.
Research with free questions instead of fixed categories

I started with a batch tool that searches fixed categories by region. On paper it made sense. In the test app I saw that choosing from fixed categories can make you miss good spots, and in the interviews nobody described searching from a fixed list. So I built the research as free questions to the AI. The results land on the map right away, and I decide on each one.
Shortlisting with a quick keep or skip. Add ratings later.

In the interviews, one traveler said he wanted to go through spots quickly, like swiping: like or dislike. So every find gets a fast keep or skip first, and ratings come later, once a shortlist exists. The alternative was rating every place the moment it appeared. Rating pins at all is a big step up from MyMaps, which has nothing like it, and it turns the kept finds into a shortlist I can build days from.
Advanced route planning with built-in time management

In MyMaps, a route was a list of stops. In Vayo, drive times between places show instantly and add up per day and for the whole trip. I added a start time for each day, so I can see whether a day can be done while the sun is still up. For that I needed the time spent at each place. Google's API has it, but it costs extra. Then I had the idea to ask the AI that was already connected to the app. It finds the time at no extra cost, and I can still change it.
Planning a full trip in weeks instead of months

The final design brings the whole funnel into one place: research with free questions, a shortlist built by keeping or skipping, and day plans with drive times and a sunset check. Everything sits on one map, so nothing has to be copied from one tool to the next.
Key wins
These numbers come from my own trips. I planned a full 4-week trip with Vayo. So far only I have used it, so I can't yet say how it works for anyone else.

If I did it again, I would start discovery from what I already knew. I had years of my own trips and years of conversations with friends about how they plan, and none of that went into the research. I treated the topic as unknown, so the discovery phase repeated things I could have started from.
